Name: metaphor_scaffolding_bias
Title: Reasoning on Metaphorical Rails: Do LLMs Inherit and Depend on Conceptual Metaphors Baked Into Language?
Short Hypothesis: LLMs inherit conceptual metaphors from language (e.g., MORE IS UP, GOOD IS UP, TIME IS HORIZONTAL SPACE, QUANTITY IS SIZE) and use them as covert reasoning scaffolds: problems framed congruently with the culturally-dominant metaphor are solved MORE accurately and faster, while metaphor-incongruent (but logically identical) framings systematically degrade accuracy and induce predictable directional errors. This reveals that part of LLM 'reasoning' is parasitic on metaphorical structure embedded in language rather than on abstract, metaphor-independent computation.
Related Work: Kramer (2025, 'Conceptual Metaphor Theory as a Prompting Paradigm') uses CMT prompts to IMPROVE reasoning, treating metaphor as a helpful add-on, and does not test whether metaphors act as an involuntary bias. Cognitive science (Lakoff & Johnson; Boroditsky on space-time metaphors; Casasanto on mental-number-line and good-is-up) establishes that humans reason along metaphorical mappings and show congruency effects. In LLMs, prior work studies spatial reasoning benchmarks, number-line/anchoring biases, and framing effects piecemeal, but none (1) systematically catalogs a set of conceptual metaphors and tests each with matched congruent/incongruent-but-logically-identical framings, (2) treats metaphor congruency as a causal manipulation predicting a directional error signature, or (3) tests whether stripping/reversing the metaphor removes a reasoning crutch. My prior proposals cover typology, content-vs-length, naming, pivot language, invented dialects, narrative order, obligatory marking, structural transfer, and underspecification; none address conceptual metaphor as an inherited reasoning bias. This proposal isolates a specific, testable mechanism of language-shaped cognition in machines.
Abstract: Human languages encode abstract concepts through pervasive conceptual metaphors: more is up, good is up, the future is ahead/to-the-right, quantity is size. Cognitive science shows humans reason faster and more accurately when tasks align with these metaphorical mappings, and make directional errors when they conflict. Because LLMs are trained on human text saturated with such metaphors, we ask whether they inherit these mappings as covert reasoning scaffolds, so that 'reasoning' becomes partly parasitic on metaphorical framing rather than metaphor-independent computation. We construct reasoning problems (numeric comparison and arithmetic, temporal ordering and scheduling, evaluative/preference ranking, and spatial-quantity mapping) each rendered in three logically-identical framings: metaphor-CONGRUENT with the culturally-dominant mapping (e.g., larger numbers positioned higher/rightward; better options 'up'), metaphor-INCONGRUENT (mapping reversed), and metaphor-NEUTRAL (no spatial/evaluative language). We evaluate open models (Llama-3, Qwen2.5, Gemma-2, Aya) and test three predictions: (i) accuracy is highest for congruent framings and lowest for incongruent, with neutral in between; (ii) incongruent errors are directionally predictable (biased toward the metaphor-default answer), a signature distinct from random noise; (iii) forcing the model to explicitly restate the problem in metaphor-neutral form before solving recovers most of the incongruency-induced loss, showing the metaphor was doing covert work. We further probe whether the effect scales with reliance on implicit (vs explicit) metaphor and correlate congruency effects with attention to metaphor-bearing tokens. Results would reframe part of machine reasoning as riding on metaphorical rails inherited from language, informing prompt robustness, benchmark fairness, and theories of language-thought coupling.
Experiments: 1) METAPHOR-KEYED TASK SUITES (~150 problems each) targeting four well-attested conceptual metaphors: (a) MORE IS UP / QUANTITY IS VERTICAL-OR-RIGHTWARD SPACE—numeric comparison and simple arithmetic where quantities are described with spatial/size language and layout; (b) TIME IS HORIZONTAL SPACE (future = ahead/right)—temporal ordering and scheduling; (c) GOOD IS UP / BETTER IS HIGHER—evaluative ranking and preference/decision problems; (d) QUANTITY IS SIZE—comparisons where larger cardinality is described with size adjectives. Each problem has an automatic verifier and a well-defined correct answer independent of framing. 2) THREE FRAMINGS per problem, logically identical: CONGRUENT (matches dominant mapping, e.g., 'the taller bar has more', better option placed 'above'), INCONGRUENT (mapping reversed, e.g., 'the taller bar has fewer', better option placed 'below'/'left'), NEUTRAL (no spatial/evaluative metaphor; plain relational statements). Validate that only the metaphorical framing changed and content/difficulty are matched via automated equivalence checks and human spot-checks. 3) MAIN EFFECT: for each of 4 open models, measure final-answer accuracy per framing; fit mixed-effects logistic regression correct ~ framing + task + log(#tokens) + (1|problem) + (1|model), predicting CONGRUENT > NEUTRAL > INCONGRUENT; report effect sizes and per-model congruency effect (congruent minus incongruent accuracy). 4) DIRECTIONAL-ERROR SIGNATURE: on INCONGRUENT problems, test whether errors are biased toward the metaphor-DEFAULT answer (the answer that would be correct under the congruent mapping) far above chance; compare error direction distribution to the random-error null via a binomial/permutation test. This distinguishes a genuine metaphorical bias from generic difficulty. 5) CAUSAL DE-METAPHORIZATION: prompt the model to first restate the problem in metaphor-neutral, purely relational terms, then solve; measure % of incongruency-induced accuracy loss recovered. Include a token-matched 'restate as-is' control to rule out extra-computation confounds. Predict large recovery if the metaphor was a covert crutch. 6) MECHANISM (support): with CoT enabled, measure whether reasoning traces explicitly invoke the metaphor (spatial/evaluative language) more under congruent framings, and whether trace-metaphor-mention mediates the congruency effect (mediation analysis); optionally examine attention mass on metaphor-bearing tokens. 7) GENERALIZATION/SCALING: test consistency across all four metaphors and two model sizes per family; report metaphor × framing interactions. METRICS: accuracy per framing, congruency effect size, directional-error bias rate vs null, de-metaphorization recovery %, trace-metaphor-mention mediation effect; all via mixed-effects models with CIs.
Risk Factors and Limitations: 1) Constructing congruent/incongruent framings that are truly logically identical yet differ only in metaphor is delicate; incongruent phrasings may be inherently more confusing/disfluent, confounding metaphor with fluency—mitigated by fluency/naturalness validation, the neutral condition, and the directional-error test (a fluency confound would not produce metaphor-directional errors). 2) The dominant metaphor direction can be culture/language-specific (e.g., rightward vs leftward time); we anchor to English-dominant mappings and treat cross-linguistic variation as a follow-up. 3) De-metaphorization prompting adds tokens/serial compute; addressed with the token-matched restate control. 4) Effects may be small or model/scale-specific; multiple models/sizes and effect-size reporting address this. 5) Attention-based mechanism evidence is only supportive; the behavioral mediation and directional-error analyses carry the causal weight. 6) A null congruency effect would still be informative, indicating current LLMs reason in a metaphor-independent way—itself a meaningful contribution to the language-thought question.
